summary.title: StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a $15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling

setting_and_object.category: System / Runtime artifact (with an accompanying failure-driven optimization methodology)

details: Long-horizon agents fail on complete jobs even when the model can solve each constituent step: plans get diluted in long traces, mutable state must be reconstructed from append-only history, lessons from prior runs are not reactivated, and agents self-declare completion prematurely.

The paper asks how much apparent model failure is actually harness failure, framing 'harness scaling' (improving the execution layer with frozen model weights) as an axis complementary to model scaling.

StateM: an agent-native runtime whose control layer is a human-readable, versioned YAML runbook (states, permitted transitions, in/out hooks, transfer checks, guards, recovery paths) that a general-purpose CLI agent operates through its ordinary command line, while the runtime holds authoritative execution state outside the model context.

Crux: each state is simultaneously a context boundary (entry refreshes phase-local instructions and durable progress) and a contract boundary (a checked, logged 'goto' protocol that refuses to commit a transition until exit conditions pass, routing to repair otherwise); checks are typed by evidentiary strength (host-executed command/predicate vs. agent self-attestation vs. LLM review).

Accompanying method: failure-driven harness optimization, in which postmortems of runs are abstracted into versioned 'practices' (prompts, checks, activation rules, repair paths), so procedural knowledge accumulates outside model weights; the runbook is jointly inspectable/editable by agent and user.
Terminal-Bench 2.1: 89 tasks, 5 trials each (445 trials); primary metric trial success rate, plus five-trial task coverage (tasks solved at least once).

BusinessBench: 477 eligible instances across 7 task families; one family-specific profile developed on a development split and frozen before the first held-out one-shot evaluation; 405 instances across 6 families treated, attendance-payroll deliberately abstained.

Profile development may use visible task specs, workspace artifacts, public docs, and observable execution feedback, but explicitly not hidden tests, verifier code, solutions, task hashes, or task-identifier routing keys.
Cost accounting separates adaptation expenditure from final-evaluation expenditure; submission-pipeline model cost reported separately from realized API charges.
Codex-based agents with GPT-5.5 xhigh, GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh, GPT-5.6 Luna, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash; statem-Codex agent version 0.144.1 for the public submission.
Terminal-Bench control profile developed with GPT-5.5, then frozen (no target-model-informed changes) for GPT-5.6 Sol/Luna; DeepSeek gets an explicitly permitted adaptation phase.
BusinessBench: GPT-5.6 Luna task agents propose changes from failure traces; a GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh hyper-agent judges family-level generality before reconciling into the frozen profile.
Human input supplies high-level architecture and 'golden rules' (minimal reusable control, route from visible task semantics, separate development feedback from frozen evaluation).

Published/public reference scores for the same models with plain Codex: GPT-5.5 xhigh 83.1%, GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh 84.9%, GPT-5.6 Luna 76.7%, GPT-5.6 Sol ultra 91.9%, Sol max 88.8% (score-only) with a $574.68 public submission at 83.37% raw.
DeepSeek-V4-Flash baseline (82.7%) measured by the authors.
Note that reference rows are model-matched public results, not agent-version-matched A/B reruns.
Runs mostly on a personal Codex Pro plan and MacBook Pro M4; formal submission run on AWS m7i.4xlarge for environment compatibility; total personal budget under $125 of a $200 plan.
95.28% is raw pre-adjudication; scoring four disputed trajectories as zero gives 94.38%, all nine flagged gives 93.26%; PR not merged.

DeepSeek full-suite result reported three ways: 392/445 standard timeout, 392/440 on an 88-task common core excluding gpt2-codegolf, and a descriptive 395/445 aggregate after extending the timeout for that single task.

key_findings.finding: A better harness with frozen model weights yields a gain larger than the observed model-generation upgrade on Terminal-Bench 2.1.
key_findings.evidence: GPT-5.5 xhigh + StateM reaches 92.1% versus the 83.1% GPT-5.5 Codex reference (+9.0 points) with 88/89 five-trial coverage, while the reference harness moves only 83.1% to 84.9% from GPT-5.5 to GPT-5.6 Sol (+1.8 points); GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh + StateM records 424/445 = 95.28% raw with 89/89 coverage, +10.4 over its 84.9% reference.

key_findings.finding: Transfer of procedural control is hierarchical: exact profiles transfer across nearby model generations, but only the runtime, structure, and development principles transfer across providers.
key_findings.evidence: The GPT-5.5-developed profile frozen without change lifts GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh (84.9% to 95.28%) and GPT-5.6 Luna (76.7% to 85.4%, exceeding the 84.9% Sol xhigh reference), yet directly applied to DeepSeek-V4-Flash it slightly hurts (82.7% to 82.0%); after provider-specific adaptation of concrete practices DeepSeek reaches 88.09% (392/445).

key_findings.finding: Harness adaptation moves the cost-accuracy frontier by orders of magnitude, making a cheap model competitive with frontier configurations.
key_findings.evidence: DeepSeek final-score evidence cost $15.20 in realized API charges (adaptation $37.02; total $52.22) versus $574.68 model cost for the public GPT-5.6 Sol max submission (83.37% raw), roughly 1/37.8 and 1/11 respectively; the descriptive DeepSeek aggregate 395/445 = 88.76% matches the reported 88.8% Sol max score at one decimal.

key_findings.finding: Task-side generalization follows mechanism match rather than task diversity: aggregate held-out gains are modest, while families whose execution boundary matches the encoded controls improve sharply.
key_findings.evidence: On BusinessBench's first frozen held-out evaluation, family macro improves 84.67% to 85.22% (+0.55) and instance micro 84.44% to 85.78% (+1.34), while Budget Approval rises 62.91% to 75.12% and Machine Operating 90.79% to 100.00% (subgroup macro +10.04); development split improves +5.64 and all treated instances +3.96.

key_findings.finding: Negative transfer arises from attaching control to the wrong execution boundary, not from insufficient control, so experience must be filtered before becoming durable memory.
key_findings.evidence: RefactorBench (80.56% to 77.78%) and WooCommerce (92.59% to 88.89%) regressed under the first profiles; post-evaluation matched reruns with thinner obligation-closure and cross-system-invariant profiles improved RefactorBench 76.39% to 79.17% and WooCommerce 86.42% to 90.12% (held-out 85.37% to 90.24%); the authors also document memorizing evaluator conventions (left-most DNA insertion boundary, video frame-precision defaults) as an undesirable learned practice.
